title: Learning to read music and advice on ear training
summary: He began reading about 1918 with Pops Foster from method books; he advises learning to read while still practicing playing by ear.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Well, when you first started and you had these people helping you, Jules and others, did you ever get a method book? Never did.
I never began to read music until I got on about 1918.
Then you still didn't get a regular method to start on, I guess?

No, I didn't get a guitar method, I just got a music method. I first got a piano catechism. Yeah. And I learned the notes there, and how to build chords, first, third and fifth. I worked them out on the guitar. And then I bought a guitar method. George, George, Pop Foster, he and I bought a method at the same time. He bought a bass method. It was 1918, when we got in St. Louis. He bought a bass method, and I bought a guitar method. And we went to work on them.
Who was it? You telling us that other guys in the band would be running around at night, but you always...

Yeah, they'd be at either the showbiz club or the jazz lamp. And we'd be in the room wrestling with those books. And I think we didn't understand why we'd have some of the guys in the band, you know, doing intermission. We'd carry out books with us. And the guys would give us the pointers on...
Would you advise young players starting the day to learn to read right away, or to play by ear for a while, or what do you think this has been?
Well, I'd advise them to learn how to read.
Right off the reel, yeah. Well, this is an age now that you have to know how to read. You can't get by like we just get by nowadays.
Well, maybe it might be that some of you fellas learned better, I mean, turned out to be the greatest players...
Well, we had better ear training.

Now, I would advise, while learning to read, to practice playing by ear. Because the ear training is the best you can get for dance music. See, the classic music at the time varies so, that it would really be hard to train the ear. You'd have to write music for that. But in playing dance music, ear training is very valuable. It's very valuable. And it gives you a sense of rhythm, a sense of division, a sense of time. Because we played syncopations back in time when I was a youngster. And the musicians, I mean good musicians, couldn't write. They just couldn't get that division. Because they're doing it now, the guys are there writing a thing you can play. And tell you what you play, you do while they're writing it. But at that time, the guys, they were trained in one, or there was a certain rule that they were educated in music by, and that rule held good. And they worked by that rule. And then what we were playing was, they were considered outlaw. See? And it was just a different category than they were taught altogether. And they just couldn't, oh I don't know, just couldn't understand the division, not enough to write it.
And yet they had all those complicated rhythms in there. And they were taught.

Yes. After the guy just developed rhythm of his own, you know what I mean? Just hit him and he had something in him, he just let him give out with it. And if it's just good, well, at least the band tell him to do it again.
